findings.topic: India nominal GDP path (USD) - IMF WEO
findings.finding: IMF DataMapper (WEO series NGDPD) projects India's nominal GDP at US$3.909T (2025), US$4.060T (2026), US$4.521T (2027), US$4.996T (2028), US$5.542T (2029), US$6.130T (2030), US$6.744T (2031). Implied crossing years: $5T in 2029, $6T in 2030; $7T is NOT reached within the IMF horizon (ends 2031 at $6.74T).
findings.source_title: IMF DataMapper - GDP, current prices (NGDPD), India
findings.publisher_or_authors: International Monetary Fund (World Economic Outlook database)
findings.date: Accessed 2026-10-24; values match press reports of the October 2026 WEO (2026 $4.06T, 2027 $4.52T, 2028 $4.996T)
findings.verified_how: fetched_api (JSON values read directly). Edition label not in API response; October 2026 WEO attribution cross-checked against search snippet of a 19-Oct-2026 news report (newsbytesapp, page itself returned 403).

findings.topic: IMF revision: $5T milestone slipped due to rupee
findings.finding: IMF Oct-2026 revision cut India's 2028 nominal GDP to $4.996T from ~$5.1T six months earlier, pushing $5T to 2029; driver is exchange-rate assumption (INR ~95.5/USD in 2028 vs 93.3 in April projection), not weaker rupee-terms growth.
findings.figure: 2028: $4.996T (prev ~$5.1T); INR 95.5/USD assumed for 2028
findings.source_title: Weak rupee delays India's $5 trillion economy goal to 2029
findings.publisher_or_authors: NewsBytes (reporting IMF WEO Oct 2026)
findings.verified_how: search_snippet only (page returned HTTP 403). GDP numbers independently confirmed via IMF API (A1); INR assumptions NOT independently verified.

findings.topic: IMF Nov-2025 India consultation: $5T in FY29
findings.finding: IMF consultation report released 26 Nov 2025 projected India to hit $5T in FY29, a year later than previously projected; FY28 at $4.96T.
findings.source_title: IMF thinks India's $5 trn economy goal will take one more year. Here's what changed
findings.publisher_or_authors: Business Today
findings.verified_how: fetched_secondary (Business Today page fetched). Primary IMF report not opened.

findings.topic: Government of India: $7T by 2030 aspiration
findings.finding: Finance Ministry review (led by CEA V. Anantha Nageswaran): 'India can aspire to become a USD 7 trillion economy in the next six to seven years (by 2030)'. Business Today headline frames it as $7.3T by 2030. Note: IMF Oct-2026 data put 2030 at $6.13T, so the $7T-by-2030 aspiration is now well above IMF baseline.
findings.figure: $7T by 2030 (aspirational)
findings.source_title: Indian economy poised to hit $7.3 trillion by 2030: Finance Ministry report ('The Indian Economy - A Review', Jan 2024)
findings.publisher_or_authors: Business Today, reporting Ministry of Finance / Office of CEA
findings.verified_how: fetched_secondary (quote read on Business Today page). Primary MoF PDF not opened.

findings.topic: Current nominal GDP (INR) - MoSPI
findings.finding: MoSPI Provisional Estimates (5 June 2026, new 2022-23 base series): 'Nominal GDP, or GDP at current prices, has been estimated to attain a level of Rs 346.36 lakh crore in 2025-26', growth 8.9%; real GDP growth 7.7% (vs 7.1% in 2024-25).
findings.figure: FY2025-26 nominal GDP Rs 346.36 lakh crore (+8.9%); real growth 7.7%
findings.source_title: India's Q4 GDP expands 7.8%, taking full-year growth to 7.7%: Govt data
findings.publisher_or_authors: Outlook Business (reporting MoSPI); real growth also confirmed on All India Radio News (newsonair.gov.in)
findings.verified_how: fetched_secondary (Outlook Business page) + fetched newsonair.gov.in for 7.7% real growth. MoSPI press release itself not opened.

findings.finding: Standard Chartered research projected India becoming a $6T economy by 2030.
findings.source_title: India set to become $6 trillion economy by 2030: Standard Chartered research
findings.publisher_or_authors: Hellenic Shipping News (reporting Standard Chartered)
findings.verified_how: search_snippet only. Prefer IMF A1 for the $6T year.

findings.topic: Bloom et al. - management RCT productivity effect
findings.finding: Randomised management consulting in large Indian textile firms: published abstract reports 'adopting these management practices raised productivity by 17% in the first year'; treated firms opened more plants within three years. NBER WP (Jan 2011) version reported productivity +11% and annual profitability +about $230,000.
findings.figure: +17% productivity in first year (QJE); +11% productivity and ~+$230,000/yr profit per firm (NBER WP 16658)
findings.source_title: Does Management Matter? Evidence from India
findings.publisher_or_authors: Nicholas Bloom, Benn Eifert, Aprajit Mahajan, David McKenzie, John Roberts - Quarterly Journal of Economics 128(1):1-51
findings.verified_how: 17%: fetched_page (CEP/LSE abstract page quoting the QJE abstract). 11% and $230,000: fetched_pdf_text (NBER WP 16658).

findings.topic: Bloom et al. - owners time-constrained (68 hrs/week)
findings.finding: 'A major reason is that the owners were severely time constrained, working an average of 68 hours per week already. There was also evidence of procrastination in that some owners would defer on taking quick decisions.'
findings.figure: Owners worked avg 68 hours/week
findings.source_title: Does Management Matter? Evidence from India (NBER WP 16658)
findings.publisher_or_authors: Bloom, Eifert, Mahajan, McKenzie, Roberts
findings.verified_how: fetched_pdf_text (verbatim, NBER WP p.26-27). Not checked whether wording is identical in final QJE version.

findings.topic: Bloom et al. - inability to delegate / trust limits firm size
findings.finding: 'In every firm in our sample only members of the owning family have positions with major decision-making power over finance, purchasing, operations or employment... The principal reason is that family members do not trust non-family members.' 'As a result of this inability to delegate, firms can expand beyond the size that can be managed by a single director only if other family members are available...' Number of brothers and sons of the leading director correlates 0.689 with total employment vs 0.223 for management score.
findings.figure: Correlation 0.689 (male family members vs employment) vs 0.223 (management score vs employment)
findings.source_title: Does Management Matter? Evidence from India (NBER WP 16658), Section VII.C
findings.publisher_or_authors: Bloom, Eifert, Mahajan, McKenzie, Roberts
findings.verified_how: fetched_pdf_text (verbatim). Published QJE abstract (via CEP page) also states limits on managerial time constrained growth/reallocation.

findings.topic: Bloom et al. - information barriers and delegation after better data
findings.finding: 'Our results suggest that informational barriers were a primary factor in explaining this lack of adoption.' About 15% of practices were not adopted because firms were not aware of them; incorrect information accounted for slightly over 45% of initial non-adoption. Better management 'increased decentralization of decision making, as better information flow enabled owners to delegate more decisions to middle managers.' Owner lack of time/low ability/procrastination accounted for ~10-12% of non-adoption in experimental plants pre-intervention (23.5% in non-experimental plants).
findings.figure: ~15% not aware; >45% incorrect information; owner-time/procrastination 10.3% (treatment), 11.6% (control), 23.5% (non-experimental) one month before
findings.source_title: Does Management Matter? Evidence from India (NBER WP 16658), abstract, Sec VII.B, Table
findings.publisher_or_authors: Bloom, Eifert, Mahajan, McKenzie, Roberts
findings.verified_how: fetched_pdf_text (verbatim).

findings.topic: Bandiera, Prat, Hansen, Sadun - CEO behaviour and mismatch
findings.finding: Diary data on 1,114 CEOs in six countries (Brazil, France, Germany, India, UK, US; 356 in India). Two types: 'Leaders focus on multi-function, high-level meetings, while managers focus on one-to-one meetings with core functions.' 'We estimate that 17% of sample CEOs are mismatched'; 'These inefficient assignments are more frequent in lower income countries (36% vs 5%). The productivity loss generated by the misallocation of CEOs to firms equals 13% of the labor productivity gap between high and low income countries.' Average CEO logged ~50 hours/week. CEO behaviour index significantly lower (more 'manager'-type) in Brazil and India.
findings.figure: 17% mismatched overall; 36% in low/middle-income (Brazil, India) vs 5% high-income; mismatch = up to 13% of cross-country labour-productivity gap
findings.source_title: CEO Behavior and Firm Performance
findings.publisher_or_authors: Oriana Bandiera, Stephen Hansen, Andrea Prat, Raffaella Sadun - Journal of Political Economy 128(4):1325-1369
findings.verified_how: fetched_pdf_text (NBER WP 23248, verbatim) + fetched_page (RePEc/IDEAS for JPE citation and abstract excerpts). Exact figures in final JPE text not re-checked.

findings.topic: Bandiera, Lemos, Prat, Sadun - family CEOs and hours
findings.finding: 'The comparison of 1,114 family and professional CEOs reveals that family CEOs work 9% fewer hours relative to professional CEOs. Hours worked are positively correlated with firm performance, and differences between family and non-family CEOs account for approximately 18% of the performance gap between family and non-family firms.' Sample includes 356 Indian CEOs.
findings.figure: Family CEOs -9% hours; explains ~18% of family vs non-family performance gap
findings.source_title: Managing the Family Firm: Evidence from CEOs at Work
findings.publisher_or_authors: Oriana Bandiera, Renata Lemos, Andrea Prat, Raffaella Sadun - Review of Financial Studies 31(5):1605-1653
findings.verified_how: fetched_pdf_text (NBER WP 19722 abstract, verbatim). RFS citation from search snippet.

findings.topic: Indian CEO time use (357 listed manufacturing firm CEOs)
findings.finding: Average Indian CEO recorded ~39 work hours/week; 56% of time in in-person meetings; 12% e-meetings; 12% working alone; 6% plant visits; 7% travel. Production-related people take the largest share: about 9 hours/week, or 35%. Over three-quarters of firms owned by founders/family; 68% of CEOs belong to owning family. 'Firms' productivity is higher when CEOs work longer hours but not all CEOs' time is equally productive.'
findings.figure: 35% of CEO time on production-related interactions; 56% in meetings; 68% family CEOs
findings.source_title: Managerial capital at the top: evidence on CEOs time use and firm performance in India
findings.publisher_or_authors: Oriana Bandiera, Andrea Prat, Raffaella Sadun
findings.verified_how: fetched_pdf_text (verbatim) - but preliminary unpublished draft hosted on a third-party blog; cite B2a/B2b for investor materials and use this only as directional colour.

findings.topic: Hsieh & Klenow - Indian plants barely grow with age
findings.finding: 'In the U.S., the average 40 year old plant employs almost eight times as many workers as the typical plant five years or younger. In contrast, surviving Indian plants exhibit little growth in terms of either employment or output.' Mexican 40-year-old plants employ twice as many as new plants. Life-cycle differences 'could lower aggregate manufacturing productivity on the order of 25% in India and Mexico relative to the U.S.'
findings.figure: US ~8x employment growth age <5 to 40; India ~no growth; Mexico 2x; ~25% aggregate TFP loss
findings.source_title: The Life Cycle of Plants in India and Mexico
findings.publisher_or_authors: Chang-Tai Hsieh, Peter J. Klenow - Quarterly Journal of Economics 129(3), 2014
findings.verified_how: fetched_pdf_text (NBER WP 18133 abstract, verbatim). QJE volume/issue from prior knowledge - NOT VERIFIED on journal page.

findings.topic: Porter & Nohria - How CEOs Manage Time
findings.finding: 27 CEOs (avg revenue $13.1B) tracked 24/7 for 13 weeks, 60,000 hours. 72% of work time in meetings (37 meetings/week); ~36% reactive mode 'handling unfolding issues'; 43% on activities furthering their agendas (range 14%-80%); 21% on strategy; 25% functional and business unit reviews; 25% developing people and relationships; 16% organisation/culture; 4% M&A; 11% routine duties; 75% of time scheduled in advance; 9.7 hours per weekday plus work on 79% of weekend days.
findings.figure: 72% meetings; 36% reactive; 43% agenda; 21% strategy; 25% functional/BU reviews
findings.source_title: How CEOs Manage Time
findings.publisher_or_authors: Michael E. Porter, Nitin Nohria - Harvard Business Review
findings.verified_how: fetched_page (HBR article HTML downloaded; all figures matched verbatim). Sample is large US-centric public companies, not Indian promoters.

findings.topic: India family business professionalisation (PwC 2016)
findings.finding: PwC India Family Business Survey 2016: ~1/3 planned to pass business fully to next generation (down from 40% in 2014); nearly half planned to keep family ownership but bring in professional management; 69% wanted experienced non-family managers to professionalise.
findings.figure: 69% want non-family professional managers (India, 2016)
findings.source_title: PwC India Family Business Survey 2016: Aligning with India's growth story
findings.publisher_or_authors: PwC India
findings.verified_how: search_snippet only (PDF and page both returned HTTP 403). Do not cite numbers until the PDF is opened.

findings.topic: Entrepreneur mental health (academic)
findings.finding: 'Mental health differences directly or indirectly affected 72% of the entrepreneurs in this sample' (personal history 49%; family history among asymptomatic 23%). Sample: 242 entrepreneurs, 93 comparison participants (US convenience sample). Depression 30%, ADHD 29%, substance use 12%, bipolar 11%; 32% had two or more conditions.
findings.figure: 72% affected; 30% depression
findings.source_title: The prevalence and co-occurrence of psychiatric conditions among entrepreneurs and their families
findings.publisher_or_authors: Michael A. Freeman, Paige J. Staudenmaier, Mackenzie R. Zisser, Lisa Abdilova Andresen - Small Business Economics 53(2):323-342
findings.verified_how: fetched_page (RePEc/IDEAS abstract). Peer-reviewed but small US convenience sample; not India; not specifically owners of ₹100-5,000 Cr firms.

findings.topic: Indian startup ecosystem wellbeing
findings.finding: 'State of Mind: The Startup Ecosystem' study: 823 retained responses; 47.5% of respondents recorded low wellbeing; founders 42.9% low wellbeing (employees 54.3% per search snippet).
findings.figure: 42.9% of founders low wellbeing
findings.source_title: Mental health crisis in startups: study finds 47.5% report low wellbeing
findings.publisher_or_authors: People Matters (study by Priyanka Kartari, Dr Sukhmani Pal, Dr Dilip Panniker; initiated by Sheetal Bahl)
findings.verified_how: fetched_secondary (People Matters page). Startup founders, not established promoters; methodology not reviewed.

findings.topic: Missing middle - medium enterprises share (NITI Aayog)
findings.finding: 'The sector remains largely dominated by micro enterprises, which constitute 97% of the registered MSMEs, followed by Small Enterprises (2.7%) and medium enterprises (0.3%).' Medium enterprises 'contribute 40% of MSME export income'; 67,923 medium entities, 58% in manufacturing; FY2022-23 medium-enterprise exports US$50,562.1 million.
findings.figure: Medium = 0.3% of registered MSMEs (67,923 entities) but ~40% of MSME export income
findings.source_title: Designing a Policy for Medium Enterprises
findings.publisher_or_authors: NITI Aayog (prepared by Administrative Staff College of India under NITI research grant; NITI disclaims data accuracy)
findings.verified_how: fetched_pdf_text (verbatim).

findings.topic: Dwarf firms - Economic Survey 2018-19
findings.finding: 'While dwarfs, i.e., firms with less than 100 workers despite being more than ten years old, account for more than half of all organized firms in manufacturing by number, their contribution to employment is only 14 per cent and to productivity is a mere 8 per cent. In contrast, large firms (more than 100 employees) account for three-quarters of such employment and close to 90 per cent of productivity despite accounting for about 15 per cent by number.' Body text: dwarfs' employment share 14.1%, NVA share 7.6%.
findings.figure: >50% of organised manufacturing firms are dwarfs; 14% employment; 8% productivity
findings.source_title: Economic Survey 2018-19, Vol 1, Ch 3: Nourishing Dwarfs to become Giants: Reorienting policies for MSME Growth
findings.publisher_or_authors: Ministry of Finance, Government of India
findings.verified_how: fetched_pdf_text (verbatim).

findings.topic: Counterpoint: 'missing middle' contested
findings.finding: Using microdata for India, Indonesia and Mexico: 'there is no "missing middle" in the sense of a bimodal distribution'; 'large firms, not small firms, have higher average products'; 'no economically meaningful bunching of firms near the notch points'. Implies the issue is a 'missing large/growth' problem rather than a regulatory notch.
findings.figure: Qualitative
findings.source_title: The Missing "Missing Middle"
findings.publisher_or_authors: Chang-Tai Hsieh, Benjamin A. Olken - Journal of Economic Perspectives 28(3):89-108
findings.verified_how: fetched_page (AEA abstract page).
